cap: "You just bought a Chick-fil-A — for ten thousand dollars."
"At least, that is what it feels like."
"You handed over the check."
"They handed you the keys."
(carry — the keys land; silent impact beat)

(carry — keys resting in his hands; the handover completes) [CORRECTED 2026-11-03: cars line moved to CF-004 — the brief draws 003B as keys in hands; Muse map error, Claude followed the map as delivered]
"The cars are lined up around the building, about to pay your store."
"Your store."
"Your restaurant."
"Your business."
"Except for one small thing. Chick-fil-A never calls you the owner." [plate: OPERATOR]
"They call you the operator."
"And that one different word is hiding everything — the money, the building, all of it."
"Because here is the truth under that word: you will run this restaurant for years…"
"and you will never own one piece of it."
"So we are going to do something about that missing piece."
"We are going to build the paycheck Chick-fil-A never prints — from their own paper, one dollar at a time."
"So what does the so-called owner of a Chick-fil-A actually walk away with?"
"First, you have to see why so many people want"
"the seat you are now sitting in."
"The big free-standing-style Chick-fil-A stores averaged"
"about nine point one six million dollars in sales in one year."
"That number comes from the company's own filing."
(carry — the counter rush carries it)
"And it is not a few super stores"
"pulling that number up."
"The store right in the middle sold"
"about nine point zero nine million."
"That is more than double the average McDonald's restaurant,"
(carry — the spotlit store holds)
"which made about four point zero six million."
"And Chick-fil-A does it while closed on Sundays."
"Every Sunday the doors stay shut —"
"and the store still brings in more money"
"than almost any other fast food place in America."
"That is the dream people see."
"A packed store, a line that never stops — and a price to get in that sounds like a joke."
"Ten thousand dollars."
"Most big franchises ask for more money than a house costs."
"Which is why the line to get in is not at the drive-thru."

"It is at the door. So why don't you just walk through that door and buy one?" [Alignment corrected 2026-11-03: captions re-anchored to the brief's picture order — chart (013) carries the distribution line, comparison picture (016) carries McDonald's number, calendar/closed-Sunday pictures (017/018) carry the Sunday lines, tags (020) carry the price lines. Edit notes: CF-013's chart plate takes NO number (bars only); CF-015's plate stays blank (spotlight visual only).]
"You are not the only one who had this idea."
"More than forty thousand people apply"
"to run a Chick-fil-A every year."
"About seventy-five to eighty of them get picked."
"Less than one person out of every five hundred gets in."
"And having the ten thousand dollars"
"does not move you to the front of that line. Chick-fil-A is not looking for an investor."
"An investor puts in money, then sits back and collects a check."
"They are looking for someone who will run the store himself —"
"you, in the building, full time, hands on."
(carry — the refusal holds)
"They pick the person."
(carry)
"Then that person pays the ten thousand."
"And even that ten thousand is not all spent."
"Half of it — five thousand dollars — is a deposit."
"The company holds it while you run the store,"
"and settles up with you when you leave."
"It is a job you have to be chosen for —"
"that you then pay to start."

"But hold on. If all you paid was ten thousand dollars… who pays for the restaurant?" [Alignment corrected 2026-11-03: check-on-desk (030) now carries the deposit line; vault slot (031) carries the settle-up line.]
"That is exactly the right question."
"The company's own paper lists the starting costs of a new store."
"The total runs from about three hundred eighteen thousand dollars"
"to almost three point five million."
"But look at what is NOT on that list."
"No line for the land."
"No line for the building."
"No line for building the store at all."
"Chick-fil-A handles that part itself." [rows highlight]
"The company finds the spot, buys it or rents it," [gap zone circled]
"and the building goes up before the operator ever gets the keys."
(carry)
(carry — the deed signing plays out the company securing the spot)
(carry)
(carry — the finished building stands before the operator arrives)
(carry)
"Your list is different: your ten thousand dollar fee, the first food,"
"the first month of rent, insurance, money to run on at the start."
"That ten thousand is the only check you write up front to get the keys."
(carry — the checklist ticks off the starter list)
"After that, the store runs on the money the store itself brings in —"
"and you pay rent to the company every month for the building you work in."
"In a normal franchise, the owner borrows a huge pile of money,"
"builds the store, and takes the big risk."
"If the store fails, the debt is still his."
"Here, the company takes that risk."
"And when one side pays for almost everything… that side keeps almost everything."

"It explains every number that comes next." [Alignment corrected 2026-11-03 (second pass, from Claude's sheet-9 catch, verified against the images brief): CF-040–041B are carries (deed + finished building play under the company-secures-the-spot lines); your-list lines sit on CF-042/042B (arrival with suitcase + check); the only-check line sits on the CF-043 flat-lay (check + key); store-money line on CF-044, rent line on CF-044B (rent check changing hands); normal-franchise lines on CF-045/045B (buried owner); fail lines on CF-046/046B (failed store); pays-for-everything lines on CF-047 (company holding land + model); bridge line on CF-047B.]
"Let's follow one hundred dollars."
"A customer pays one hundred dollars at the counter."
"Chicken, fries, drinks."
"Before anyone else gets paid, Chick-fil-A takes fifteen dollars."
"Not fifteen percent of the profit —" [$15 slice peels]
"fifteen dollars out of the whole one hundred, right off the top."
"That rule is in the company's filing: fifteen percent of all sales."
"That slice also covers rent for the kitchen gear"
"and a small monthly fee for company services — it all comes out of the same fifteen."
"Fifteen percent of nine point one six million is about"
"one point three seven million dollars a year to the company side — before costs, before profit, before you see a cent from that slice."
"That is cut number one — and at the end of both cuts sits the number this whole hunt is for." [bar full height]
"Okay. Eighty-five dollars are left."
"Now the real costs come out: the chicken, the bread, the potatoes, the cups,"
"the people who cook and serve, the lights, the insurance,"
(carry — the cook station holds the people line)
"and the rent for the building — paid to Chick-fil-A, because the building is theirs."
(carry — the rent envelope holds)
"Up to about three dollars and twenty-five cents more can be set aside for ads, under the deal."
(carry)
"Whatever is left after all of that is the profit."
"And here comes the second cut: Chick-fil-A takes half of that too."
"To be exact, the paper first sets aside a small base amount for the operator — one thousand dollars a month —" [pile splits]
"and then the rest of the profit is split down the middle."
"Half to the company. Half to the operator."
"So the company gets paid twice:"
"once on every sale, even if the store makes no profit at all,"
"and again on half the profit."
"You get paid last — only from what survives both cuts."
(carry)
(carry)
(carry — section out-breath)

(carry) [Alignment corrected 2026-11-03: ads line moved onto the billboard (058), profit line onto the small pile (059), split explanation onto the split state (060), payoff line onto the mascot's face crop (063B).]
"Here is the honest answer —"
"the one almost nobody tells you straight."
"Chick-fil-A does not publish what you would make."
"It is not in the filing."
"The filing reports sales — and only sales."
"No profit. No owner pay. Anywhere."
"Anyone who gives you one exact pay number,"
"and says it like it is a fact, is guessing."
"That missing number is the one number Chick-fil-A never has to tell anyone."
"Outside companies have tried to work it out from the costs."
"Their guesses for a typical store land roughly between"
"one hundred eighty-seven thousand and three hundred thousand dollars a year."
"Read that the right way: that is their estimate, not a promise from Chick-fil-A,"
"and a busy store and a slow store will not land in the same place."
"But even at the low end, you can see why people want in."
"You paid ten thousand dollars to start."
"You did not borrow millions to build a store."
"And you can end up with a pay level most store managers never reach."
"That is the good part of the deal. And it is real."
"Now here is the part that is just as real."
(carry)
(carry)
(carry)
(carry)
(carry — mood turns toward S7)
"In most franchises, the owner is building something he owns."
"Year after year, his store becomes worth more. One day he can sell it, or hand it to his kids."
"You get none of that." [four labels appear one by one: LAND / BUILDING / EQUIPMENT / THE BUSINESS — CHICK-FIL-A'S; let this shot hold while the labels land]
(carry — the generic owner's calendars and rising arrow play out the praise)
(carry)
"The land is the company's."
"The building is the company's."
"The kitchen gear is the company's."
"Even the company that runs the restaurant belongs to Chick-fil-A."
"You cannot sell the business, because it was never yours to sell."
"You cannot pass it to your kids, because you never owned it."
"And for a long time, most people in your seat ran just one store —"
"so you cannot grow the way other owners do,"
"by opening a second and a third."
"Your money is only the pay."
"The year you stop running that store, the money stops too."
"You spent years building one of the busiest restaurants in the country. And the thing you built belongs to someone else."
(carry — the for-sale sign with the X plate)
(carry)
"And you do not have to run a restaurant to know this feeling."
(carry)
(carry)
(carry)
"A big title that makes it sound like you own something — while someone else owns everything under it."
"Almost everybody has lived a small piece of that story."
"You can pay ten thousand dollars, and maybe —"
"out of forty thousand people — be the one they pick."
"You will run a store that sells millions."
"The company will take fifteen cents of every dollar first, and half the profit after that."
"You will never own the store."
"And forty thousand people will still line up next year for the chance."
"Because if you are one of the few who get picked, the trade is simple:"
"you give up owning the business,"
"and in return you skip the million-dollar debt"
(carry)
"and step straight into the busiest fast food store in the game."
"That is why the cheapest franchise in America costs ten thousand dollars."
"It is not cheap because it is small."
"It is cheap because there is nothing to buy."
"You are not paying for a restaurant."
"You are paying to be chosen to run one."
(final line echoes — keys in the open hand; no new words)
(carry)
